en: Homage to Mañjuśrī, the Ever-Youthful.
The *Tri-svabhāva-nirdeśa* composed by the master Vasubandhu:
The imagined, the dependent, and the perfected.
The three natures are held by the wise to be the profound object of knowledge.

That which appears is the dependent nature; the manner in which it appears is the imagined nature, because its activity is dependent on conditions and because it exists as mere conceptual construction.
The perpetual non-existence of that which is so described, exactly as it is described,
should be known as the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because it is unchanging.
In that regard, what is it that appears as the "unreal imagination"? How does it appear as having a dual nature?
What is its non-existence by virtue of which there is the state of non-duality therein?
In this context, there is some unreal conceptualization by which something is conceptualized;
and in whatever way it conceptualizes an object, in that very way it does not exist at all.
By way of being cause and effect, the mind is held to be twofold:
that which is called the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and that which is called the evolving-consciousness (pravṛttivijñāna), which is sevenfold.
It is called "mind" (*citta*) because it is accumulated by the seeds of the latencies of affliction;
the first is the mind itself, while the second is so called because it functions in diverse forms.
In brief, this unreal imagination is considered to be of three kinds: that which is maturational, that which is conditional, and another which is apparitional.
The first is the root-consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), because it consists of maturation (*vipāka*);
the other is the evolving-consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*), due to the process of the perception of the object and the perceiving subject.
The profundity of the natures is intended on account of existence and non-existence, duality and unity, and the lack of distinction in the characteristics of affliction and purification. (Tsn 10)
Since the imagined nature is grasped by the mind as being absolutely non-existent,
it is therefore considered to have the characteristic of both existence and non-existence.
Because it exists as an illusory state yet does not exist in the manner in which it appears,
the dependent nature (paratantra) is therefore considered to have the characteristic of being both existent and non-existent.
Because it exists as non-duality and because there is the very absence of duality,
the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is therefore considered to have the characteristic of both existence and non-existence.
Because the imagined object is twofold, yet exists solely as its non-existence,
the imagined nature is considered by the foolish to consist of both duality and unity.
Because it appears as a duality and because it consists solely of error,
the nature called the dependent (paratantra-svabhāva) is considered to have the essence of both duality and unity.
Because its nature is the absence of duality, and because it has the single nature of non-duality,
the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is considered to consist of the identity of duality and unity.
The imagined and the dependent are to be known as the characteristics of affliction;
the perfected, however, is held to be the characteristic of purification.
Because it has the nature of the non-existence of the two unrealities, and because its nature is the absence of those [two],
the perfected nature should be known as non-different in character from the imagined nature.
Because its intrinsic nature is non-duality, and because its intrinsic nature is the absence of duality,
the perfected nature and the imagined nature should be understood as having an undifferentiated characteristic.
Because it does not exist in the manner in which it is described, and because it has the nature of non-existence in that way,
the perfected nature (niṣpanna-svabhāva) is characterized as non-different from the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
Because it lacks the nature of the two unrealities and because its nature is not as it appears,
the dependent nature should be understood as having a characteristic non-different from the perfected nature.

The sequential differentiation of the intrinsic natures is established for the sake of instruction, based on the requirements of conventional usage and for the purpose of facilitating entry into that [reality].
The imagined nature is the essence of conventional discourse; another is the essence of the one who engages in discourse;
and yet another is held to have the nature of the cessation of conventional discourse.
First, the dependent nature, which consists in the non-existence of duality, is entered; then, one enters therein that which is mere conceptual construction—the unreal duality.
Then, the existence of the non-existence of duality is entered as the perfected nature;
for it is precisely this that is then said to be both "existent" and "non-existent."
For these three natures have the characteristic of being non-dual objects;
because they are non-existent, because they do not exist as such, and because their nature is the absence of that [duality].
Just as that which is produced by illusion through the power of mantras appears in the form of an elephant—
therein exists only the appearance, but the elephant does not exist at all.
The imagined nature is the elephant; the dependent nature is its appearance;
that which is the absence of an elephant therein is held to be the perfected nature.
In the same way, an unreal construction appears from the root-consciousness in the form of duality;
duality does not exist at all there, for only the mere appearance exists.
Root-consciousness is considered to be like a mantra, suchness like a piece of wood;
conceptual construction is to be regarded as the form of an elephant, and the duality as the elephant itself.
Upon the penetration of the reality of the object, the three characteristics—
full knowledge, abandonment, and attainment— are intended simultaneously, in their respective order.
In this context, thorough knowledge is the non-perception [of objects], while abandonment is held to be non-manifestation;
attainment, however, has perception as its cause, and it is also direct realization.
Through the non-perception of the duality, the appearance of duality vanishes;
through its disappearance, the perfected nature, which is the absence of duality, is realized.
Just as in a magical illusion, there is simultaneously the non-perception of an elephant and the disappearance of its form, along with the perception of wood.
Because contradictory cognitions are excluded, because the futility of cognition is perceived, and because the three types of knowledge persist, liberation would be attained without effort. (TSn 35)
Through the perception of mind-only, there is the non-perception of knowable objects;
through the non-perception of knowable objects, there is the non-perception of mind.
Through the non-apprehension of both, there is the apprehension of the dharmadhātu;
through the apprehension of the dharmadhātu, there is the apprehension of mastery.
And having attained mastery through the accomplishment of the welfare of oneself and others,
the wise one attains unsurpassed enlightenment, which consists of the three bodies.
Thus ends the exposition of the three natures.
This is the work of the venerable master Vasubandhu.
